description:
Hacker used a spoofed phone number.  Called me from an 800 number that I thought was from a legitimate business I was working with at the time. Immediately knew my name and said he was from the HQs Security Office of Wells Fargo Bank in San Francisco.  I questioned the phone number and he told me to look on the back of my credit card and the number called when there is an issue is the number he was calling from.  It was spoofed but I didn’t know that then.  He said my account and others were in jeopardy and the branch I use had been compromised by an insider.  I know that Wells Fargo has had an issue with insiders before so thought it was possible for sure.  I questioned him further and he then sent a spoofed text from WF and also proceeded to tell me everything that was in my checking and savings accounts.  He had it all.  I “thought” no one would be able to get that info unless it was a Wells Fargo office so unfortunately believed him at that point.  He asked me to help flush out the insider by sending a fake wire transfer.  He said no money would be taken (it was) and that it had to be a large amount to entice the insider.  I tested him again by saying I don’t have that much in my account and he said, “yes you do, you have xxx in your savings account” which was the exact amount.  When I went to send the wire, a woman came in soon after and was upset that her account was frozen and she could not pay bills.  This could have been a coincidence or part of the scam to make it seem real.  The man had told me the police and FBI were waiting to make an arrest.  He called me the next morning as promised and told me 2 people had been arrested and he and his manager had been working on the paperwork for a while.  I asked to talk to his manager because I was definitely wondering at this point and he said
the manager would call me back in 15 minutes.  I knew this was a scam then and immediately went to the bank to report it, then to the police, who also submitted it to the FBI.  Nothing has been done by anyone.  The first thing the bank manager told me is that a hacker can get into anything!  It became totally my fault because I had answered the spoofed phone number.
Banks cannot protect your accounts, hackers can spoof numbers and texts and read every line in your account to you on the phone - so when that happens it is difficult to hang up.  I have not spoken to a hacker/scammer before and the amount of high tech items he used and a well thought out, practiced scam allowed him to steal a lot of hard earned money.  The banks do not do enough to protect our accounts but I thought they did so it is up to the consumer, account holder, to protect ourselves. The banks make sure they take no responsibility.  I would not have been scammed IF the hacker had not been able to completely get into my account.  This hacker/scammer could be awarded an Oscar for his high tech computer skills combined with acting (lying) skills so do not become a victim like I did.

description:
A man called, claiming to be with the Chase Bank fraud department.  He asked me to confirm whether 2 suspicious Zelle transitions were legitimate.
When I told him that they were not, he proceeded to give me claim numbers that I needed to use in Zelle to cancel the pending transactions, and then transferred me to a man claiming to be with Zelle.  The second man gave me instructions on how to go into my banking app, open the Zelle transfer dialog, and send the cancellation codes in order to cancel the transactions.
At this point I told him that I wasn't going to send those and told him that I suspected he was a scammer.  He immediately threatened me by saying that if I didn't enter the cancellation codes, he was going to release the transactions.
The way Zelle works is that money can be sent to someone or requested from someone.  Apparently the scammers had identified my phone number as having both a Chase account and a Zelle account. The apparently initiated a request for money from me, which apparently generated confirmation codes for me to use to complete the transactions.  If I had sent those confirmation codes, some amount of money would have been transferred from my bank account.
The danger here is that unlike PayPal or Venmo, Zelle transfers money immediately from one bank account to another almost immediately.  With Zelle, there is no realistic way to reverse the transfer.  Often the scammers use compromised accounts and immediately withdraw the transferred funds and deposit them into another bank account, most likely offshore where US jurisdiction doesn't have protections.  This makes recovery almost impossible, ergo the inability to reverse a Zelle transaction such as this.
The way I knew that it wasn't Chase Bank calling me was that I have fraud protection on my accounts and Chase alerts me of potential fraud in a very different manner.  However, for people who do not have such protections, and may not have ever interacted with Chase or other financial organization, they could be convinced that this was a genuine call and followed through with the instructions provided.
My advice is that if someone claiming to be from a bank or credit card company calls to alert you about fraud, thank them for the alert and then hang up and call the real bank or credit card company using the phone numbers printed on the credit card or listed in a reliable resource.  Once they answer, let them know that someone contacted them to alert them of potential fraud and ask to speak with someone from their fraud department.  If the alert was genuine, the fraud department will work with them to address the issue.  If it is a scam, the fraud department will confirm that there isn't any suspicious activity.

description:

They falsely claimed to offer "permanent outdoor Christmas lights" with specific, high-quality features: individual, covered sequence lights in a square form, along with regular cables and individual attachments designed to withstand harsh environmental conditions. Their advertisement even included a video of someone receiving four bulky boxes of lights that matched the characteristics they promoted.
After seeing this, I placed an order for the same set of four boxes. However, what I received was nothing like what was advertised. Instead, I was sent an envelope containing four small packages of mini LED lights that are clearly a safety hazard for outdoor use, given their poor quality and unsuitability for electronic connections.

The product was shipped from China, and my research shows that the company is actually based in Singapore. This inconsistency raises serious doubts about the legitimacy of their information.
I feel completely scammed and have reported the company to the Federal Trade Commission for false advertising. Additionally, their website lacks essential information such as an address, phone number, and return policy, making it clear that it's a fraudulent site. I am taking action because they continue to advertise on social media, and PayPal has failed to provide a satisfactory solution. It's time to hold this scammer accountable.

description:
I met an individual on the dating app Bumble, and we developed a romantic relationship. Approximately one month into the relationship, he suggested that I invest in an e-commerce business through a platform called Podazz.club. This business model appeared to operate as a dropshipping venture where I was required to fund product orders. I was assured that once the orders were delivered, I would receive a refund of my investment along with a profit.
Initially, I was able to withdraw some funds, but I was informed that withdrawals were only possible if no pending orders existed. Encouraged by the initial success, I proceeded with two larger orders, for which I took out loans to fund. The platform operators then claimed that some of my transactions were flagged for money laundering activities and demanded an additional $70,000 for account review. They assured me that this amount would be deposited back into my account after review.
Subsequently, I was asked to pay an additional $30,000 as a fine, followed by another $30,000 in penalties. I did not pay the final $30,000, at which point the individual I had been communicating with admitted that the entire operation was a scam. He informed me that the perpetrators were located in Taiwan and that the platform operated using cryptocurrency, making recovery of my funds unlikely.
In total, I deposited approximately $300,000 into the platform before discovering it was fraudulent. I am seeking legal action against the perpetrators and assistance in recovering my funds.

description: I Googled recipes and clicked on the first one. Immediately on my screen was a starburst saying WARNING, and a very loud noise came through my laptop. The screen said it was a result of a scammer trying to get to my computer, but don't worry b/c i called the phone number on my screen. The message was that they were subcontractors for Microsoft, and would help me safeguard my system. I believed them, especially since the screaming noise ended. I spent 2 hours with them as they copied info off my system. The pages flashed by quickly, but i took some photos of what they took. They assured me I would be ok. Then they presented me with prices for protection, starting at $399. The five-year $2196 seemed the best option, so i took it. They told me to write a check, and to put it on my printer. Then they controlled my wifi; i watched my printer scan the check as they took it. They said they can "protect" everything I have that's on WiFi, don't worry. They can access and protect my phone/laptop/printer/tv. They were very nice, and their "contract" seemed legit--even warning against other scams! I later called my bank to say stop payment, b/c I wasn't feeling good about this. Bank said, don't worry, we have 24/7 fraud department (it really was my bank). I trusted that I'd be ok. But I mentioned it to a friend, and he said I was scammed. He told me to have my pc wiped by a very reputable computer firm in town; and they did that. They made my pc look as though it were new, out of the box, nothing on it but Windows 11. Later i found out more and this company is very very well known and relied on. I changed my bank accounts, all my autopays, and my credit card--it took me days to change all my passwords. The scammers kept leaving me voicemails that I ignored. The last one warned they were sending me to collections, b/c the bank didn't honor my check (I'd also submitted a local police report; that, plus my recorded conversation with the bank, in which they said not to worry, they have 24/7 fraud protection) helped me get my money back. [the bank told me it's impossible to find fraud--they process millions of payments every day]). Today i see in the mail that they're sending me what is likely a threatening letter. I won't sign for it, if thats required for receipt. Everything i see online about Global Bytes IT (or IP) Solutions points to its being a fraud. Even Microsoft's website says it's a fraud--MS uses no contractors, and you cannot phone MS and that it's a scam if a company claims to be subcontractor. I'm lucky: I got my money back. But that's rare, i understand.
